title: A GHIC or EHIC card doesn't replace travel insurance — here's the gap it leaves
excerpt: A GHIC or EHIC only gives access to state-provided healthcare in the EU at local rates — it doesn't cover repatriation, private treatment, cancellation, or anything outside the EU.
body: A UK Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC) or the older EHIC is genuinely useful — it entitles you to state-provided healthcare in the EU on the same terms as a resident of that country. It's also one of the most commonly misread pieces of paper in UK travel planning, because 'covers state healthcare' quietly gets rounded up to 'covers me on this trip.'

The gap starts with what a GHIC/EHIC doesn't touch at all: it has no cancellation cover, no baggage or gadget cover, and nothing for a trip outside the EU. Within the EU, it only applies to state-provided care — if the nearest suitable treatment is private, or the country's state system doesn't cover a specific treatment for its own residents either, the card doesn't help.

The largest gap is repatriation. If a medical emergency means getting flown home for treatment or because you're unfit to fly commercially, that cost sits entirely outside what a GHIC/EHIC provides — and repatriation is precisely the scenario proper travel insurance's medical cover is built around.

None of this makes the card worth leaving at home — it's a genuinely useful backstop for EU state care and worth carrying alongside insurance, not instead of it. The medical excess on a travel policy (what you pay first if you claim for treatment abroad) is a separate, smaller cost that sits on top of, not in place of, that wider protection.

The same logic applies whether it's a single-trip policy for one holiday or an annual multi-trip policy for several — either way, check the GHIC/EHIC is treated as a supplement to the policy's medical cover, not confused for a substitute for it.
